title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: Horizontal Scaling
summary: Horizontal scaling (or "scaling out") means adding more machines/instances to a pool to handle increased load, in contrast to vertical scaling (Topic 12), which makes a single node bigger.
objectives: What is horizontal scaling and how does it differ from vertical scaling?
Why is consistent hashing preferred over naive modulo hashing for distributing keys across nodes?
What is a shared-nothing architecture and why is it important for horizontal scalability?
How do stateless and stateful services differ in their ability to scale horizontally?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Horizontal scaling (or "scaling out") means adding **more machines/instances** to a pool to handle increased load, in contrast to vertical scaling (Topic 12), which makes a single node bigger.

Horizontal scaling is the strategy that lets modern internet services grow to sizes that no single machine could ever serve. Instead of buying one enormous server, you deploy thousands of small, interchangeable servers and distribute work across them. The moment you add a new node, aggregate capacity goes up; the moment you remove one, it goes down. This elasticity is the backbone of cloud-native design and the only practical way to absorb traffic that swings 10× between 03:00 and 21:00. The seminal real-world example is **Netflix**, which runs over 100,000 EC2 instances across three AWS regions and autoscales them by the thousands every evening when subscribers start streaming, then releases them overnight to cut cost. No single machine on Earth could serve Netflix's peak traffic; only horizontal scaling can.

The key enabler is whether a service is **stateless** or **stateful**. Stateless services — web front-ends, API gateways, stateless microservices — scale out trivially. Any instance can serve any request because nothing is remembered between calls. A load balancer (Topic 3 covers the broader scalability story; here we focus on the distribution layer) spreads requests round-robin or by least-connections, and you can add or remove instances without coordinating with the others. Kubernetes makes this almost frictionless: bump the `replicas:` field in a Deployment and the scheduler places new Pods on available nodes within seconds. Netflix's playback recommendation API, Amazon's product page service, and Uber's trip-dispatch front door are all stateless services that scale horizontally to tens of thousands of instances.

Stateful services are harder. A database cannot just "add a node" because the new node has no data yet. You need **sharding** (also called **partitioning**): split the dataset by some key (user ID, region, time range) and assign each shard to a different node. New nodes either take over a subset of existing shards (rebalancing) or accept writes for new shards going forward. The classic technique is **consistent hashing**, which minimizes data movement when nodes are added or removed — only `1/N` of keys move when the cluster grows from N to N+1 nodes, instead of the naive modulo approach where nearly all keys would remap. **Cassandra** is the canonical example: it uses consistent hashing with virtual nodes (vnodes, typically 256 per physical node) to achieve near-linear horizontal scalability. Apple famously ran a Cassandra cluster of over 75,000 nodes storing tens of petabytes of message data; Instagram uses Cassandra for feeds and direct messages on a cluster of similar scale.

The **shared-nothing architecture** is the ideal: each node owns its own CPU, memory, and disk, and there is no contention for shared resources. Shared-nothing systems scale linearly because adding a node adds a full unit of independent capacity. The opposite — shared-disk architectures like a clustered file system on a SAN — eventually bottleneck on the storage controller and don't scale horizontally despite having many compute nodes. This is why modern horizontally scalable databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB, ScyllaDB, MongoDB sharded cluster) all adopt shared-nothing: each shard owns its data and its disks, and cross-node coordination is minimized to gossip, replication, and the occasional rebalance.

Load balancers are the traffic cops of horizontal scaling. At Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), HAProxy, AWS NLB, or IPVS distribute by connection. At Layer 7 (HTTP), NGINX, Envoy, or AWS ALB can route by URL path, cookie, or header — useful for canary releases and sticky sessions. For stateful services you often want **consistent hashing at the LB layer too**, so that all requests for `user_42` land on the same backend that caches their data — this is how Instagram's feed service keeps cache hit rates above 95% despite hundreds of backend instances. Modern service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) push this further with client-side load balancing and locality-aware routing that prefers same-AZ backends to cut cross-AZ bandwidth costs.

The trade-offs of horizontal scaling are real. First, **operational complexity explodes**: 100 instances means 100 places for failures, 100 OS patches to schedule, 100 logs to aggregate, 100 metrics to correlate. Netflix built the entire Simian Army (Chaos Monkey, Latency Monkey, Conformity Monkey) precisely to tame this complexity by continuously injecting failures. Second, **distributed-systems pathologies appear**: you now have CAP (Topic 10) and PACELC (Topic 11) trade-offs, network partitions, clock skew, split-brain, and eventual consistency. Third, **cost models change**: many small instances cost more per unit of compute than one big one — a fleet of 100 `m5.large` instances costs roughly the same as one `m5.24xlarge` but delivers less raw CPU due to per-instance overhead. The break-even comes from elasticity: you can release the 100 small instances at 02:00, while the big box runs 24/7.

A common pitfall is **stateful services masquerading as stateless**. A web app that stores session data in local memory "scales horizontally" on paper but loses sessions on every deploy, can't be load-balanced without sticky sessions, and breaks under failover. The fix is to externalize state into a shared cache (Redis, Memcached) or a database, then any instance can serve any request. Another pitfall is **uneven sharding** ("hot shards"): if you shard by first letter of username, the letter "S" gets 5× more users than "Z" and one node saturates while others sit idle. Cassandra's vnodes and Instagram's power-of-two choices algorithm both mitigate this by spreading each node's load across many virtual positions on the ring.

Horizontal scaling connects deeply to the rest of the curriculum. It is the only path to high **availability** (Topic 4) beyond a single machine — you can survive AZ and region failures. It enables high **throughput** (Topic 9) via parallelism, at the cost of cross-node **latency** (Topic 8) for coordination. It demands careful **consistency** choices (Topics 10 and 11). And it pairs with **load testing** (Topic 14) to validate that the autoscaler actually adds capacity under real load, then with **SLOs** (Topic 15) to measure whether the scaled-out service meets its reliability targets. In practice, the right strategy is almost always: vertical-scale until you can't (Topic 12), then horizontal-scale out — and design for horizontal scaling from day one even if you start small.

   ADD a node N3:   only ~1/N keys move (e.g. 1/3 of ring)

### Walkthrough
1. Traffic arrives at a load balancer, which routes each request to one of N backend nodes. For stateless services the choice is arbitrary (round-robin, least-connections); for stateful services the LB uses consistent hashing on a request key (user ID) so the same node always serves the same user.
2. Each backend node owns a slice of the data — a shard. Writes go to the owning node and are replicated to N-1 peers for durability and failover. Reads are served locally or via quorum depending on the consistency model (CAP/PACELC, Topics 10–11).
3. An autoscaler watches a metric (CPU, queue depth, request rate) and adds or removes nodes. New nodes fetch their assigned shard from existing replicas (a process called "bootstrapping" in Cassandra or "rebalancing" in Kafka) and start serving traffic. Removed nodes hand off their data and shut down. Consistent hashing keeps the data movement to ~1/N of the keyspace on every membership change.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes (vnodes).
# Demonstrates add/remove node behavior, key distribution, and data movement.

import hashlib
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

def _hash(s: str) -> int:
    """Stable 64-bit hash from MD5 (deterministic across runs)."""
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).digest()[:8], "big")

@dataclass
class ConsistentHashRing:
    """A consistent hash ring with configurable virtual nodes per physical node."""
    vnodes: int = 150
    ring: List[Tuple[int, str]] = field(default_factory=list)  # (hash, node_id), sorted
    node_ids: set = field(default_factory=set)

    def _re_sort(self) -> None:
        self.ring.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])

    def add_node(self, node_id: str) -> int:
        """Add a node; return the number of keys that would move."""
        if node_id in self.node_ids:
            return 0
        # Compute the before-state for movement accounting.
        before = [self._owner(k) for k in range(0, 10000)]
        for v in range(self.vnodes):
            h = _hash(f"{node_id}#{v}")
            self.ring.append((h, node_id))
        self.node_ids.add(node_id)
        self._re_sort()
        after = [self._owner(k) for k in range(0, 10000)]
        moved = sum(1 for b, a in zip(before, after) if b != a)
        return moved

    def remove_node(self, node_id: str) -> int:
        """Remove a node; return the number of keys that would move."""
        if node_id not in self.node_ids:
            return 0
        before = [self._owner(k) for k in range(0, 10000)]
        self.ring = [(h, n) for (h, n) in self.ring if n != node_id]
        self.node_ids.discard(node_id)
        after = [self._owner(k) for k in range(0, 10000)]
        moved = sum(1 for b, a in zip(before, after) if b != a)
        return moved

    def _owner(self, key) -> str:
        if not self.ring:
            return ""
        h = _hash(str(key))
        # Find first ring slot whose hash >= h (clockwise walk).
        for slot_hash, node_id in self.ring:
            if slot_hash >= h:
                return node_id
        return self.ring[0][1]  # wrap-around

    def distribution(self, keys: List[str]) -> Dict[str, int]:
        counts: Dict[str, int] = {n: 0 for n in self.node_ids}
        for k in keys:
            counts[self._owner(k)] = counts.get(self._owner(k), 0) + 1
        return counts

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ring = ConsistentHashRing(vnodes=150)
    keys = [f"user_{i}" for i in range(10000)]

    for n in ["N1", "N2", "N3"]:
        moved = ring.add_node(n)
        dist = ring.distribution(keys)
        print(f"Added {n}: keys_moved={moved}, dist={dist}")

    # Remove a node — only ~1/N keys should re-map, not all.
    moved = ring.remove_node("N2")
    dist = ring.distribution(keys)
    print(f"Removed N2: keys_moved={moved}, dist={dist}")

    # Compare with naive mod-N hashing on the same membership change.
    def naive_owner(key, nodes_sorted):
        return nodes_sorted[_hash(key) % len(nodes_sorted)]

    before = {k: naive_owner(k, ["N1", "N2", "N3"]) for k in keys}
    after = {k: naive_owner(k, ["N1", "N3"]) for k in keys}
    naive_moved = sum(1 for k in keys if before[k] != after[k])
    print(f"Naive mod-N would have moved: {naive_moved}/{len(keys)} keys")
```

quiz.explanation: Horizontal scaling ("scaling out") adds more machines to a pool to share load, while vertical scaling ("scaling up", Topic 12) makes a single machine bigger. Horizontal scaling trades operational simplicity for elasticity and fault tolerance: you can survive single-node failures, autoscale with demand, and grow beyond the largest available instance type.

quiz.question: Why is consistent hashing preferred over naive modulo hashing for distributing keys across nodes?
options: First, cache aggressively — put the celebrity's feed in Redis with a short TTL (e.g., 5 seconds); 99% of reads hit the cache, sparing the database.
The problem is uneven distribution — some users generate 100× more traffic than others, and mod-16 hashing doesn't account for that.
Stateless services scale out trivially — any instance can serve any request because nothing is remembered between calls.
Naive modulo hashing maps a key to node hash(key) % N.
quiz.explanation: Naive modulo hashing maps a key to node hash(key) % N. When N changes (a node is added or removed), nearly every key remaps to a different node — catastrophic for a database that must physically relocate data. Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a virtual ring; a key maps to the next node clockwise.
